title: The letter of victory
hook: from the wilderness the Guru writes to the emperor Aurangzeb in Persian, rebuking broken oaths
tomorrow: Nanded, 1708: the Guru is the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chali Mukte, the forty who left and came back, and the paper the Guru tore up. Your line was you can always come back. Did you hold a door open for someone? Day ninety-two.
screen: `CHALI MUKTE — YOU CAN ALWAYS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time someone broke a promise to you and you finally sat down to write back. Most of us write that letter twice. The first draft is all fury. The second one, the one we send, is shorter and harder to argue with. Now picture a man who has lost almost everything. His city is gone. His mother is gone. All four of his sons are gone, two in battle and two behind a wall. He's in a small village in the dry country of Punjab, with a handful of followers. And he picks up a pen and writes to the most powerful man in India, the emperor Aurangzeb. He calls it a letter of victory.
screen: `THE LETTER YOU WRITE TWICE.` → `EVERYTHING LOST.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Zafarnama. Zafar is victory, nama is a letter, or a book. The letter of victory. Guru Gobind Singh wrote it in Persian, the language of the Mughal court, in verse: a little over a hundred couplets. Tradition says two Sikhs, Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh, carried it hundreds of miles south to the emperor's camp in the Deccan. It opens the way a letter to a king would, with praise, but the praise isn't for the king. It's for God. Then it turns to the emperor, and it doesn't flatter. At Anandpur, the letter says, your commanders swore oaths, on the Qur'an itself, that the Guru and his people could leave in safety. And the moment they left, they were attacked. The Guru writes as someone who takes an oath seriously, and holds the emperor to his own faith's promise. The letter's most famous line says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Sikhs read it carefully: not a love of fighting, but a last resort, after every other door is shut. So why victory? The Guru had no army to speak of and no home. The victory is in the telling. Truth, said plainly, to the face of power, by a man with nothing left to lose. Tradition says the emperor was shaken by it, and that he died not long after, in 1707. Historians aren't sure he ever read it. Sikhs keep it in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings linked to the tenth Guru, and still read it aloud.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA — THE LETTER OF VICTORY.` · `IN PERSIAN, TO THE EMPEROR.` · `YOU SWORE ON THE QUR'AN, AND BROKE IT.` · `THE SWORD ONLY WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.` · then, large: `VICTORY IS THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly for a moment. Think of something true you haven't said. Maybe to someone who let you down. Maybe to someone you let down. Maybe just to yourself. Now find one sentence for it. Not the angry draft. The short one. Clear, honest, without cruelty. If you have paper, write it down. If not, say it once, silently. You don't have to send it. Just let it be true, and let it be yours. The bell holds the time.
Zafarnama. The letter of victory, written in Persian by Guru Gobind Singh to the emperor Aurangzeb, holding him to his broken oaths.
Your line: victory is the truth. Today, write one honest sentence, and cut every word from it that's there to hurt. Day ninety-two.

screen: `DAY 92 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NANDED, 1708: THE GURU IS THE GRANTH.`

howItsDone: The Zafarnama is kept in the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs read and recite it, often in the original Persian, especially when remembering the events of 1704 to 1706.

fork.setup: you've lost your home, your mother and your four sons, all after a promise of safe passage was broken. you write to the emperor who made it. what do you write?
options: a plea for mercy and a new truce.
a curse on him and all his house.
praise of God, then the plain truth about his broken oaths.
fork.reveal: the Zafarnama opens with praise of God, then holds the emperor to his oaths. the Guru called it a letter of victory.

original.note: Persian, in Perso-Arabic script: zafar, victory, and nama, a letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a boast after winning a war.
what it means: a letter from a man who had lost nearly everything, telling an emperor the truth about his broken oaths.
what a scholar hears: Persian verse, a little over a hundred couplets, preserved in the Dasam Granth; whether it ever reached Aurangzeb is debated.

sources.ref: Zafarnama (Dasam Granth), on the broken oaths and the sword as a last resort

notes: Number of couplets: commonly given as 111 (some count differently); the script says 'a little over a hundred'. Confirm.
Place and date of composition: tradition places it at Dina (Kangar), around 1705-06; the script says only 'a small village in the dry country'. Confirm the order relative to Khidrana (day 91).
The 'last resort' couplet is paraphrased, not quoted; no public-domain translation was used. Confirm the paraphrase.
'All four of his sons are gone' before the letter: consistent with days 89-90; confirm.
Oaths sworn on the Qur'an (and, in some accounts, by the hill rajas on the cow): the script mentions only the Qur'an. Confirm that framing is fair and handled respectfully.
Whether Aurangzeb read the letter is historically uncertain; stated so.
